newsitem.title: USA: New HK leader vows to work toward smooth transition.
newsitem.headline: New HK leader vows to work toward smooth transition.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa vowed to work toward a smooth transition from July 1 when China takes control of Hong Kong, ending 156 years of British colonial rule.

In a television interview taped in Hong Kong and aired in the United States on Tuesday night, Tung emphasized that citizens in Hong Kong will retain key rights guaranteeing freedom of expression, movement and capital flows, as well as the right to demonstrate.
But he said he would not allow the former British colony to be used as a staging area for efforts to attack China.
"I will not permit Hong Kong to become a base to destabilize China," Tung said in an interview broadcast on U.S. public television's "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer."

"This is not acceptable to a large group of people in Hong Kong because it is not in Hong Kong's interest to permit this. Certainly it is not in China's interest to do this. This cannot be permitted," Tung said.
Tung, appointed by Beijing, is to swear in the Provisional Legislature in the early hours of July 1 after a midnight handover ceremony returning the colony to Chinese control.
The interview was conducted by Britain's Independent Television Network. Tung spoke in English.
Tung repeated earlier statements urging Hong Kong to "leave behind the baggage" of the Tiananmen Square demonstrations eight years ago to focus on the future.

Western diplomats in Beijing believe that hundreds, possibly several thousand, people died June 3 and 4, 1989, mostly when they tried to stop convoys of troops from passing through the city to the central square where students and other demonstrators had gathered.

"I want to be sure that we are happy, that Hong Kong is going to go through a smooth transition," he said. "Let us put aside June 4. Let us look to the future and build an even better Hong Kong for our children."
Beijing hails the return of Hong Kong as marking the end of more than 150 years of colonial humiliation and has promised a high degree of autonomy for the territory's 6.4 million people.

But many U.S. politicians and other international observers have been concerned by the effect on Hong Kong's political freedoms of its transfer to Communist control and have angered Beijing by threatening economic penalties if liberties are rolled back.
